## Example

Use mobility $\mu>0$, stiffness $k>0$, and fixed bath temperature $T_b>0$. Under the adopted linear bath model, the stationary position spectrum has angular-frequency convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stationary Gaussian preparation of the specified linear model.

[F1] [[post-td-linear-ornstein-uhlenbeck-bath]]: $\gamma=\mu k$ and $\sigma^2=2\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b$.

[F2] [[pthm-td-ornstein-uhlenbeck-thermal-fluctuations]]: $C(\tau)=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k)e^{-\mu k|\tau|}$ and the exact model spectrum is known.

## Verification

**Given:** $\gamma=\mu k>0$ and $V=k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k$.

1.1 Substituting $V=k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k$ and $\gamma=\mu k$ into the exact spectrum supplied by [F2] gives $S(\omega)=\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\pi[(\mu k)^2+\omega^2])$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The same supplier bound becomes $\operatorname{Var}(T^{-1}\int_0^T X_tdt)\le2k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\mu k^2T)$, which tends to zero as $T\to\infty$. Both formulas are conditional model predictions, not measurements. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

At a stipulated common $T,p$, let one mole of a component occupy phase $\alpha$ with molar volume $v_\alpha=1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$ or phase $\beta$ with $v_\beta=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. Consider a separated mixture of total amount $N=2\,\mathrm{mol}$ and total volume $V=5.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}$; use the volume convention of [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] and additivity of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Both phases are present, their molar volumes and the mixture totals are as in the Example, and volume and amount are additive for this separated compound.

[F1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] and [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]: For one component, the phase amounts add to $N$, and the separated phase volumes add to $V$.

## Verification

1.1 Let $\lambda_\beta:=n_\beta/N$ and $\lambda_\alpha:=n_\alpha/N$. Positivity and amount additivity give $\lambda_\alpha+\lambda_\beta=1$, with both fractions in $(0,1)$. Volume additivity gives
$$
\bar v:=\frac VN=\lambda_\alpha v_\alpha+\lambda_\beta v_\beta.
$$
All terms have units $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Here $\bar v=2.5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. Solving the affine relation in step 1.1 yields
$$
\lambda_\beta=\frac{\bar v-v_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}=\frac12,\qquad \lambda_\alpha=\frac{v_\beta-\bar v}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}=\frac12.
$$
The fractions are positive and sum to one, so $n_\alpha=n_\beta=1\,\mathrm{mol}$ satisfies the given total amount and volume. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite integers, open coordinate domain, $C^1$ chemical-potential coordinate functions, coexistence equations, and nonsingular-minor assumptions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative-matrix entries.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: a $C^1$ map whose derivative has a specified invertible square minor has a local zero set that is a graph over the remaining coordinates, of dimension ambient dimension minus equation count.

[L2] [[thm-algebra-of-total-derivatives]]: finite sums and differences of $C^1$ real-valued maps are $C^1$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $P\ge2$, $F$ has one scalar component for each pair $(i,\alpha)$ with $1\le i\le C$ and $2\le\alpha\le P$, so it has $q=C(P-1)$ components. Each is a difference of $C^1$ maps and therefore $F$ is $C^1$ on the open set $U$ by [F1, L2]. The assumed minor lets [L1] apply, giving local graph dimension $n-q$. Expanding $n=2+P(C-1)$ gives $n-q=2+PC-P-CP+C=C-P+2$. [F1, L1, L2, given, algebra]

1.2 If $P=1$, no phase-equality equations are indexed because there is no $\alpha\ge2$. The local solution set is all of the open domain $U$, which has $n=2+(C-1)=C+1=C-P+2$ coordinates. [given, algebra]

2.1 In the reactive variant, each added affinity is a finite linear combination of $C^1$ coordinate functions and is therefore $C^1$ by [F1, L2]; the combined map has $q+R$ scalar equations. Its stated minor satisfies [L1], so the graph dimension is $n-q-R=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)-R=C-P+2-R$. Linear independence of the $\nu^r$ identifies $R$ distinct reaction directions, while the full-rank minor remains a separate necessary assumption on the equation derivatives. [F1, L1, L2, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the entropy of each phase is $C^2$ on its physical state chart and its derivative-defined temperature at the endpoint is finite and positive. The equation-set dimension below concerns this smooth interior state only.

Let $C\ge1$ be the number of named species, $P\ge1$ the number of coexisting phase branches, and $R\ge0$ the number of independent internal reaction directions. Consider an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For each phase $\alpha$, use an intensive phase branch from [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] and an interior composition $x^\alpha\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}$. Let each branch chemical-potential map
$$
\mu^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)=(\mu_1^\alpha,\ldots,\mu_C^\alpha)
$$
be $C^1$ on a common open domain
$$
\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times(\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ})^P \subseteq\mathbb R^{\,n},\qquad n=2+P(C-1).
$$
Assume energy, volume, and every named species can be exchanged between every phase pair in both directions, and every listed reaction direction is feasible in both extent directions in every phase while that phase's energy, volume, other reaction extents, and all other phase coordinates are held fixed at the coexistence point. Let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent, dimensionless stoichiometric vectors, with extents measured in moles. Phase equilibrium imposes $\mu_i^\alpha-\mu_i^1=0$ for $1\le i\le C$, $2\le\alpha\le P$; internal reaction equilibrium imposes $(\nu^r)^{\mathsf T}\mu^\alpha=0$ in every phase for $1\le r\le R$. On the phase-equality locus these are the same $R$ equations in each phase, so count them once using phase 1. Put $q:=C(P-1)$ and $m:=q+R$. If $m=0$ (equivalently $P=1,R=0$), no equation is imposed and the local zero set is the whole chart, of dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2-R$. If $m\ge1$ and the combined equation map has an invertible $m\times m$ derivative minor at the solution, with $m\le n$, then the local zero set of these first-order coexistence-and-affinity equations is a graph of dimension
$$
n-q-R=C-P+2-R.
$$
This is the dimension of the equation zero set in intensive coordinates only; phase amounts and their extensive conservation constraints are not counted, and the actual stable-coexistence set may be a proper subset after additional stability constraints. If the nonsingular-minor condition fails, no dimension formula is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite integers $C,P,R$, the open positive-temperature, interior-composition chart, C1 branch chemical-potential maps, a coexistence solution, the pairwise exchange assumptions, independent stoichiometric directions, and the stated nonsingular-minor hypothesis. Mole fractions are dimensionless; each $\mu_i^\alpha$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$.

[A1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]]: Each branch is a model-supplied C1 intensive phase chart, so derivative-defined chemical potentials are independent of the phase amount and are C1 maps of $(T,p,x^\alpha)$.

[A2] Regularity hypothesis: Each phase entropy is C2 in its physical state coordinates at the endpoint, and each derivative-defined temperature is finite and positive.

[F1] [[pthm-td-intensive-coexistence-conditions]]: At an attained entropy-maximizing coexistence point, bilateral energy and volume exchange imply equal positive temperature and pressure, and bilateral species exchange implies equal derivative-defined chemical potentials across phases.

[F2] [[post-td-entropy-maximum]] and [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]: The total entropy of the separated phases is the sum of their state entropies, and the adopted stable endpoint is a global maximum on its exact feasible set.

[F3] [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: On each single-phase chart, $S_{n_j}=-\mu_j/T$ at fixed energy, volume, and other species amounts; branch temperatures are positive.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-phase-dimension]]: For C1 chemical-potential maps on the stated open intensive composition chart, the zero set of the phase-equality equations and $R$ independent affinity equations has local dimension $2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)-R$ when the combined equation map has an invertible square derivative minor of size $C(P-1)+R$. The current batch-4 carrier and its proof contract are registered; the item remains a draft and is not independently accepted.

## Proof

1.1 For $P\ge2$, define the phase-equality components $F_{i,\alpha}:=\mu_i^\alpha-\mu_i^1$ for $1\le i\le C$, $2\le\alpha\le P$. There are exactly $q=C(P-1)$ such scalar equations. By [A1], each $\mu_i^\alpha$ is C1 on the common open domain, so their finite differences are C1. By [F1], these equations hold at the stated physical coexistence point when the corresponding species exchanges are admitted; [A2] supplies the entropy regularity and positive temperatures required by that supplier. [given, A1, A2, F1, algebra]

1.2 Fix any phase $\alpha$ and reaction direction $\nu^r$. Vary only that phase's species amounts as $n^\alpha(t)=n^{\alpha,*}+t\nu^r$, holding its energy and volume and all other phase coordinates fixed; $t$ is a small extent in moles. By the stated bilateral feasibility, this curve is admitted for both signs of sufficiently small $t$. The total entropy has a local maximum at $t=0$ by [F2]. Its differentiability there follows from [A2]. The right difference quotients are nonpositive and the left difference quotients are nonnegative; the derivative is therefore zero. Additivity and [F3] give
$$
0=\frac{dS_{\mathrm{tot}}}{dt}(0)=\sum_j S_{\alpha,n_j}\nu_j^r=-\frac{(\nu^r)^{\mathsf T}\mu^\alpha}{T}.
$$
Since $T>0$, $(\nu^r)^{\mathsf T}\mu^\alpha=0$ in every phase. The equations are C1 because they are finite linear combinations of the C1 branch maps. By [F1], phase equalities make the affinity equation identical across phases, so count only the $R$ equations in phase 1. The combined map therefore has $q+R$ equations. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, construct, algebra]

1.3 The ambient coordinate dimension is $n=2+P(C-1)$. If $q+R=0$, then $P=1$ and $R=0$, so there are no phase-equality or reaction-affinity equations. The local zero set is all of the open chart and has dimension $n=2+(C-1)=C-P+2-R$. [given, algebra]

2.1 If $q+R\ge1$, apply [L1] to the combined C1 equation map using the stated invertible minor. Its local zero set has dimension
$$
n-q-R=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)-R=C-P+2-R.
$$
This conclusion is conditional on the full-rank minor; it does not follow from equation counting alone. Additional stability constraints may reduce the physical coexistence set. [given, L1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The zero-reaction case is $R=0$. On composition boundaries the open-simplex chart fails; for reactions there, one-sided tangent inequalities replace the interior affinity equalities.

## Example

Let $C=1$, $P=2$, and $R=0$. Fix $T_0=300\,\mathrm K$ and $p_0=10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, and take a common open chart around $(T_0,p_0)$. On it define the branch Gibbs potentials per mole
$$
g_1(T,p)=g_0-s_0(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_1(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2,\qquad g_2(T,p)=g_0-s_0(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_2(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2,
$$
where $g_0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $s_0,c>0$ are in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $v_1,v_2>0$ are distinct molar volumes in $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, and $\kappa>0$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$. Set $G_i=n_i g_i$ with natural Gibbs assignments $S_i=-\partial_TG_i$, $V_i=\partial_pG_i$, and $\mu_i=\partial_{n_i}G_i$; define $U_i=G_i+TS_i-pV_i$. The derivative-defined chemical potentials are $\mu_i=g_i$, and they agree at $(T_0,p_0)$. This is a candidate equation-map solution, not a claim of entropy-maximizing coexistence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two Gibbs branches and the open $(T,p)$ chart described above, with $v_1\ne v_2$. The example is a conditional equation-map model, not an experimental claim.

[A1] The common positive-temperature, positive-pressure-or-real-pressure chart has no independent composition coordinates because $C=1$.

[A2] Adopted local Gibbs model: $G_i=n_i g_i$, $S_i=-\partial_TG_i$, $V_i=\partial_pG_i$, $\mu_i=\partial_{n_i}G_i$, and $U_i=G_i+TS_i-pV_i$.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-phase-dimension]]: For $C=1$, $P=2$, $R=0$, a coexistence-equation zero with a nonsingular derivative minor has local equation-set dimension $C-P+2=1$.

[F2] [[pthm-td-regular-gibbs-phase-rule]]: In the thermodynamic application, the same rank formula is conditional on an attained stable endpoint and the stated exchange hypotheses; this example verifies only the equation-map part.

[L1] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]: A $C^1$ map between open Euclidean sets with invertible derivative at a point has a local $C^1$ inverse there.

## Verification

1.1 From [A2], at $(T_0,p_0)$, $S_i=n_i s_0$, $V_i=n_i v_i$, $U_{i,T}=n_i c$, $V_{i,p}=-n_i\kappa$, and $V_{i,T}=0$. Thus the $(T,p)$ derivative matrix of $(U_i,V_i)$ at fixed amount has determinant $-n_i^2c\kappa\ne0$, so [L1] supplies a valid local physical-coordinate chart. [given, A2, L1, algebra]

2.1 The only coexistence equation is $F(T,p):=g_2(T,p)-g_1(T,p)=(v_2-v_1)(p-p_0)=0$. It vanishes at the center and has $\partial_pF=v_2-v_1\ne0$, so the $1\times1$ minor is invertible. [given, A2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Here the ambient dimension is $n=2+P(C-1)=2$ and the equation count is $q=C(P-1)=1$. Applying [F1] gives local equation-set dimension $n-q=1$, exactly $C-P+2=1$. This verifies the regular rank conclusion, not the stable-endpoint hypotheses of [F2]. [F1, F2, A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Postulate

Adopt **C1 (equilibrium-join coherence)**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the joined state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each constituent, $J_{ij}(x,y)\sim_T x$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)\sim_T y$, using the model’s declared nested-join identifications.

C1 is an additional postulate of this completed contact branch. The source’s Theorem 4.8 is stated with T1–T4; the local conditional calibrator route uses the constituent-to-join bridge in addition to the stronger T5 range assumption. Neither fact licenses deriving C1 from $u=u_i+u_j$, from T1–T4, or from transitivity alone. The displayed source supports the contact context, not the claim that its bare printed axioms already contain C1.

## Postulate

Adopt **T5 (universal thermal-equilibrium range)**: for every ordered pair of simple systems $i,j$, each state $x$ of $i$, and every work-coordinate point $v_j$ in the projection of the state domain of $j$, there is some state $y=(u_j,v_j)$ of $j$ with $x\sim_T y$, using [[def-td-thermal-join]].

This is a quantified existence assumption for a thermal-equilibrium partner at each permitted work coordinate. It does not define a numerical temperature, assert that all systems possess the same temperature range as a real apparatus, or supply a calibration map and its uncertainty.

## Example

Take finitely many tagged simple types $i$, each with positive dimensionless coordinates $u>0,v>0$ (numerical energy and work coordinates relative to fixed units). Choose constants $c_i,r_i>0$, reference values $u_{\star,i},v_{\star,i}>0$, and $b_i\in\mathbb R$, and define

$$s_i(u,v)=c_i\log\frac{u}{u_{\star,i}}+r_i\log\frac{v}{v_{\star,i}}+b_i.$$

For a scaled tag $t i$, set its coefficients to $tc_i,tr_i,tb_i$ and its reference coordinates to $t u_{\star,i},t v_{\star,i}$, so $s_{ti}(tu,tv)=t\,s_i(u,v)$. On finite separated compounds define the relation by nondecrease of the sum of the constituent entropies. For a thermal join of $i,j$, define the joined entropy at $(U,v_i,v_j)$ as the maximum of $s_i(u_i,v_i)+s_j(u_j,v_j)$ over $u_i,u_j>0$ with $u_i+u_j=U$, and define contact equilibrium by equality of the pair entropy with this maximum. For nested joins, use the same maximum construction recursively.

This provides a nondegenerate consistency witness for the order, geometric, contact, T5, and C1 assumptions on this positive-coordinate family. It supplies no measured parameter values or empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive coordinates; fixed $c_i,r_i>0$, reference values and constants; tagged scaling as stated; accessibility is defined by entropy nondecrease; join entropy is the constrained maximum.

[F1] [[def-td-thermal-join]]: a join retains component work coordinates and sums the energy coordinate.

[F2] [[post-td-accessibility-a1-a6]]: A1–A6 are the order conditions to be checked for the example relation.

[F3] [[post-td-simple-system-geometric-axioms]]: A7 and S1–S3 are the geometric conditions to be checked.

[F4] [[post-td-thermal-join-axioms]]: T1–T4 are the contact conditions to be checked.

[F5] [[post-td-universal-thermal-range]] and [[post-td-equilibrium-join-coherence]]: T5 and C1 are separate conditions to be checked.

[F6] [[thm-exponential-two-point-convexity]]: for $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $t\in[0,1]$, $\exp((1-t)a+tb)\le(1-t)\exp(a)+t\exp(b)$; for $0<t<1$, equality holds exactly when $a=b$.

[F7] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$, and $\log(ab)=\log a+\log b$.

[F8] [[def-real-power]] and [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]: for $K>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $v^\alpha$ is differentiable for $v>0$ with derivative $\alpha v^{\alpha-1}$.

[F9] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: if $g$ is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable inside, its endpoint slope equals $g'$ at some interior point.

## Verification
**Given:** [F1]–[F5] and the construction in the Example.

1.1 For $a,b>0$, apply [F6] to $\log a,\log b$, then use [F7] and monotonicity of $\log$, to obtain $\log((1-t)a+tb)\ge(1-t)\log a+t\log b$ for $0\le t\le1$. Apply this inequality to the energy ratios $u/u_{\star,i}$ and to the work ratios $v/v_{\star,i}$; multiplying by $c_i,r_i>0$ and adding $b_i$ proves concavity of $s_i$. This verifies the convex-combination accessibility condition. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing, raising $u$ at fixed $v$ gives a strict successor, proving S1. [F3, F6, F7, algebra]

1.2 The boundary equation $s_i(u',v')=s_i(u_x,v_x)$ rearranges to $u'=g(v')=K(v')^{-\alpha}$, where $K=u_xv_x^\alpha>0$ and $\alpha=r_i/c_i>0$. By [F8], $g'=-\alpha K(v')^{-\alpha-1}$ and $g''=\alpha(\alpha+1)K(v')^{-\alpha-2}>0$. Thus $g'$ is increasing by [F9]. For $v'\ne v_x$, the mean value theorem on the interval between them and the monotonicity of $g'$ give $g(v')\ge g(v_x)+g'(v_x)(v'-v_x)$: when $v'<v_x$, both the derivative comparison and the sign of $v'-v_x$ reverse. Hence the forward sector $u'\ge g(v')$ lies above the tangent support $u'-u_x+(r_i u_x/(c_iv_x))(v'-v_x)=0$. A vertical line cannot support this sector because its work coordinate varies on both sides at an interior boundary point. If a nonvertical line with slope parameter $q$ supports there, its inequality on graph points gives $g(v')-g(v_x)+q(v'-v_x)\ge0$ for both signs of $v'-v_x$; dividing by that difference and taking limits forces $q=-g'(v_x)$. This proves uniqueness and gives $P_i=r_i u_x/(c_iv_x)$. On any closed rectangle with $u,\tilde u\le u_1$ and $v,\tilde v\ge v_0>0$, $|u/v-\tilde u/\tilde v|\le |u-\tilde u|/v_0+u_1|v-\tilde v|/v_0^2$, so the slope is locally Lipschitz. The graph over $v'>0$ is arcwise connected, proving S3. [F3, F8, F9, algebra]

1.3 Put $C=c_i+c_j$. For any split $u_i+u_j=U$, [F6] with weights $c_i/C,c_j/C$, followed by [F7], gives $$\frac{c_i}{C}\log\frac{u_i}{c_i}+\frac{c_j}{C}\log\frac{u_j}{c_j}\le\log\frac{U}{C},$$ with equality exactly when $u_i/c_i=u_j/c_j$. Since $u_i+u_j=U$, that equality forces the unique split $u_i=c_iU/C,\ u_j=c_jU/C$. Multiply by $C$ and add the constants $c_i\log(c_i/u_{\star,i})+c_j\log(c_j/u_{\star,j})+b_i+b_j+r_i\log(v_i/v_{\star,i})+r_j\log(v_j/v_{\star,j})$; the resulting inequality is exactly the pair entropy bounded by its value at that split. This proves attainment of the join maximum, T1, and reversible join splitting. For the equal-state scaled split, tagged extensivity gives $s_{ti}(tu,tv)=t s_i(u,v)$ and $s_{(1-t)i}((1-t)u,(1-t)v)=(1-t)s_i(u,v)$, so both sides have equal entropy and the other T2 clause holds. The binary join entropy is $C\log U+r_i\log v_i+r_j\log v_j+C_{ij}$ for a constant $C_{ij}$; its energy-to-coefficient ratio is $U/C=u_i/c_i=u_j/c_j$ at the maximizing split. [F1, F4, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 On each finite product the relation compares finite real entropy sums. Reflexivity and transitivity follow from the real order; adding the same spectator adds the same number to both sides; positive scaling multiplies the sums by a positive coefficient; and reversible splitting preserves the extensive sum. If $A+\epsilon_nZ_0\prec B+\epsilon_nZ_1$, then $s(A)-s(B)\le\epsilon_n(s(Z_1)-s(Z_0))$. Taking $n\to\infty$ yields $s(A)\le s(B)$ and hence $A\prec B$. This verifies the six adopted order conditions. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a single system the entropy has the displayed logarithmic form. If a nested join has energy coefficient $C$ and is joined with a system of coefficient $c>0$, the maximum calculation of step 1.3 gives the unique maximizing split at equal energy-to-coefficient ratios; substitution adds $c$ to the energy coefficient and adds the new work term. Induction over the finite joins therefore gives coefficient $C=\sum_k c_k$ and entropy $C\log U+\sum_k r_k\log v_k+C_0$ for the positive work coordinates $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$. Its boundary is $U=g(v)=K\prod_k v_k^{-\alpha_k}$ with $\alpha_k=r_k/C>0$. Direct differentiation gives, for any vector $h$, $$D^2g(v)[h,h]=g(v)\left[\left(\sum_k\alpha_k\frac{h_k}{v_k}\right)^2+\sum_k\alpha_k\left(\frac{h_k}{v_k}\right)^2\right]\ge0.$$ Thus along each segment in the positive work orthant, the derivative of $g$ is nondecreasing by [F9], and the mean value theorem gives $g(v')\ge g(v)+\nabla g(v)\cdot(v'-v)$. The forward sector $U\ge g(v)$ lies above this tangent support; uniqueness follows by applying the support inequality to graph points in each direction $h$ and $-h$, which forces the support functional to equal $\nabla g(v)$. Its finite slope components are $P_k=r_kU/(Cv_k)$; on rectangles bounded away from all coordinate axes, the quotient estimate from step 1.2 applies to each component and proves local Lipschitz regularity. ## Statement

Let $s,r\ge1$, let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{s\times r}$ be a stoichiometric matrix (column $k$ gives the signed species-amount change per unit extent of reaction $k$), and let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^s$ be initial species amounts. Extents $\xi\in\mathbb R^r$ are measured in one fixed amount unit, so $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$ has species amounts in that same unit; $\nu$ is dimensionless. The feasible extent set is the polyhedron

$$\mathcal F=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^r:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^s\}.$$

At $\xi_*\in\mathcal F$, let $J=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Define the Bouligand tangent cone $T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ to consist of all $h\in\mathbb R^r$ for which there are $t_k>0$ with $t_k\to0$ and $h_k\to h$ such that $\xi_*+t_kh_k\in\mathcal F$. Then

$$T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)=\{h\in\mathbb R^r:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J\}.$$

If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ is open with $\xi_*\in U$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable with a local minimum at $\xi_*$ relative to $\mathcal F\cap U$, then $Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$ for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$. Conversely, if $U$ is convex and $f$ is convex and differentiable on $U$, this directional inequality for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ implies $f(\xi)\ge f(\xi_*)$ for every $\xi\in\mathcal F\cap U$. If a potential $\Phi$ is differentiable on an open neighborhood of the relevant amounts and $f(\xi)=\Phi(n^0+\nu\xi)$, define $\mu_j=\partial\Phi/\partial n_j$; then

$$Df(\xi_*)h=\sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu)\cdot h.$$

The tangent-cone and optimality claims are mathematical deductions. They do not assert that a particular physical system obeys this model or is at equilibrium.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite stoichiometric matrix, initial amounts, feasible extent set, Euclidean convergence, and differentiability/convexity hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]: differentiability at $\xi_*$ gives $f(\xi_*+w)=f(\xi_*)+Df(\xi_*)w+o(\|w\|_2)$ as $w\to0$.

[F2] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: convexity of $U$ and the affine inequalities defining $\mathcal F$ keep every segment between feasible points in $\mathcal F\cap U$.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the composition of its total derivatives.

[F4] [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]: a real-valued function is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for points in its convex domain and $t\in[0,1]$.

[F5] [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]: a finite-dimensional linear map is bounded and therefore continuous.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$, and choose sequences $t_k,h_k$ from its definition. For each active $j\in J$, feasibility gives $0+t_k(\nu h_k)_j\ge0$, hence $(\nu h_k)_j\ge0$. Since [F5] makes the finite matrix map continuous, $h_k\to h$ implies $\nu h_k\to\nu h$, so $(\nu h)_j\ge0$. This proves one inclusion. [F5, given, algebra]

1.2 Conversely suppose $(\nu h)_j\ge0$ for all $j\in J$. For each inactive $j$, put $b_j=n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j>0$. If $(\nu h)_j<0$, restrict $0\le t\le b_j/[-(\nu h)_j]$; if $(\nu h)_j\ge0$, no restriction is needed. There are finitely many species, so choose a common $\epsilon>0$ no larger than all positive bounds (or $\epsilon=1$ if there are none). For $j\in J$, $n^0_j+(\nu(\xi_*+th))_j=t(\nu h)_j\ge0$; for inactive $j$, the choice of $\epsilon$ gives $b_j+t(\nu h)_j\ge0$ for $0\le t\le\epsilon$. Thus $\xi_*+th\in\mathcal F$ throughout that interval. Taking $h_k=h$ and any positive $t_k\le\epsilon$ tending to zero proves $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$. [given, choose, algebra]

2.1 By steps 1.1–1.2, every tangent $h$ has a feasible ray $\xi_*+th$ for all sufficiently small $t\ge0$. Openness of $U$ keeps the initial part of this ray in $U$. At a relative local minimum, $[f(\xi_*+th)-f(\xi_*)]/t\ge0$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$; differentiability [F1] makes its limit $Df(\xi_*)h$. Hence $Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, given]

2.2 Now assume $U$ is convex and $f$ convex and differentiable. For any $\xi\in\mathcal F\cap U$, put $h=\xi-\xi_*$. For active $j$, $(\nu h)_j=n_j(\xi)-n_j(\xi_*)=n_j(\xi)\ge0$, so step 1.2 makes $h$ a tangent direction; the segment $\xi_*+th$ also lies in $\mathcal F\cap U$ by [F2]. Let $g(t)=f(\xi_*+th)$. [F4] gives $(g(t)-g(0))/t\le g(1)-g(0)$ for $0<t<1$; as $t\downarrow0$, the left side tends to $Df(\xi_*)h$ by [F1]. If every tangent derivative is nonnegative, then $f(\xi)-f(\xi_*)=g(1)-g(0)\ge Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 For $f(\xi)=\Phi(n^0+\nu\xi)$, the affine map has derivative $h\mapsto\nu h$. By [F3], $Df(\xi_*)h=D\Phi(n^0+\nu\xi_*)(\nu h)$. ## Statement

Fix a system at a positive temperature $T_0$ and external pressure $p_0>0$. Internal reaction extents may vary in a declared feasible set, but no species crosses the system's outer boundary. The system contacts only an ideal thermal reservoir at $T_0$ and an ideal pressure store at $p_0$; all other work coordinates and excluded-energy changes are absent. Let $U$ be system internal energy in joules, $V$ volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $S$ system entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Define the constrained potential
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}:=U+p_0V-T_0S.
$$
For every admitted spontaneous endpoint change, $\Delta\Phi_{T_0,p_0}\le0$. If the system-plus-reservoir-plus-store endpoint is an attained global entropy maximum on its exact feasible set, then the corresponding system endpoint attains a global minimum of $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ over the induced feasible reaction states. This is a conditional model deduction; it does not assert that arbitrary fixed-$T,p$ reactions have this preparation or that the system reaches the minimum dynamically.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A closed system with fixed outer boundary, internal reaction extents in an explicitly declared feasible set, an ideal bath and pressure store, an isolated compound containing the system and both auxiliaries, and an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint. Amount changes are internal; the auxiliaries exchange neither matter nor any unlisted work channel.

[A1] Ideal thermal bath: for $T_0>0$, its entropy is $S_R(E_R)=S_{R,0}+E_R/T_0$ on the admitted reservoir energy interval. If heat $Q$ enters the system, $\Delta E_R=-Q$, so $\Delta S_R=-Q/T_0$.

[A2] Ideal pressure store: its energy changes by $p_0\Delta V$ when the system volume changes by $\Delta V$, and its entropy is constant. The only system work is $W_{\rm on}=-p_0\Delta V$. Thus the fixed-total-energy constraint is $\Delta U+\Delta E_R+p_0\Delta V=0$.

[A3] The system, bath, and pressure store form the isolated compound in the adopted macroscopic second-law and stable-equilibrium model. No matter crosses the compound's outer boundary; internal stoichiometric changes do not alter the ideal bath formulas.

[F1] [[post-td-first-law-energy]]: For an admitted closed process with no excluded-energy endpoint change, $\Delta U=Q+W_{\rm on}$.

[F2] [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]: The total endpoint entropy of the admitted isolated compound does not decrease.

[F3] [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]: Stable equilibrium is an attained global maximum of total entropy on the exact feasible endpoint set.

[F4] [[def-td-si-quantities]]: $U,Q,W_{\rm on}$ and $p_0V$ are in joules; $T_0$ is in kelvins; $S$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, so $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ is in joules.

## Proof

1.1 By [A2] and [F1], $\Delta U=Q-p_0\Delta V$. By [A1], $\Delta S_{\rm tot}=\Delta S-Q/T_0$, where $\Delta S$ is the system entropy change. Therefore
$$
\Delta\Phi_{T_0,p_0} =\Delta U+p_0\Delta V-T_0\Delta S =Q-T_0\Delta S =-T_0\Delta S_{\rm tot}\le0
$$
by $T_0>0$ and [F2]. The derivation does not depend on whether $\Delta n_j$ arises from an internal reaction. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 On the exact fixed-total-energy feasible set, [A1]–[A2] give $E_R=E_{\rm tot}-U-p_0V$ up to a fixed reference constant. Hence
$$
S_{\rm tot}=S+S_R =\mathrm{constant}+S-\frac{U+p_0V}{T_0} =\mathrm{constant}-\frac{\Phi_{T_0,p_0}}{T_0}.
$$
Since $T_0>0$, an attained global maximizer of $S_{\rm tot}$ is exactly a global minimizer of $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ on the induced feasible reaction states, by [F3]. [given, A1, A2, A3, F3, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The argument is the fixed-reservoir entropy bookkeeping extended to internal changes of species amounts. It does not cover an open matter reservoir, which would contribute chemical-potential terms, or an external work channel not included in [A2].

## Statement

Fix $C\ge1$ species and $R\ge1$ declared internal reaction extents. Let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{C\times R}$ be the dimensionless stoichiometric matrix, let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^C$ have units mol, and let $\xi\in\mathbb R^R$ have units mol. The amount vector is $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$, and the nonnegative-amount feasible extent set is
$$
\mathcal F_\nu:=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^R:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^C\}.
$$

Let $\Phi(\xi)$ be the constrained Gibbs potential on an open neighborhood $U$ of an equilibrium extent $\xi_*$, and assume the model supplies a finite $C^1$ extension through every zero-amount boundary point under consideration. On $U$, assume
$$
D\Phi(\xi)[h]=\sum_{j=1}^C\mu_j(\xi)(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi))\cdot h,
$$
where $\mu_j$ are the molar chemical potentials in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. This extension and derivative identity are not supplied by the positive-mole phase chart itself.

Suppose $\xi_*$ is an attained stable equilibrium for the fixed-$T_0,p_0$ internal reaction model with the ideal reservoirs of [[pthm-td-fixed-tp-reaction-potential-minimum]]. $$
T_{\mathcal F_\nu}(\xi_*):=\{h\in\mathbb R^R:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J_*\}.
$$
The first-order necessary condition is
$$
(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*))\cdot h\ge0\qquad(h\in T_{\mathcal F_\nu}(\xi_*)).
$$
If $\xi_*$ is interior to $\mathcal F_\nu$, this reduces to $\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*)=0$. If, in addition, $\Phi$ is convex and differentiable on a convex neighborhood containing the relevant feasible set, the same tangent inequality is sufficient for global minimization there.

**Given:** The finite species list, stoichiometric matrix, feasible amount set, fixed $T_0,p_0$, a local Gibbs-potential branch and the explicit C1 boundary extension and gradient identity in the Statement. ## Statement

Let an admitted refrigerator cycle in the sense of [[def-td-reservoir-cycle]] operate between fixed ideal-bath temperatures $0<T_c<T_h$, extract $Q_c>0$ from the cold bath, reject $Q_h>0$ to the hot bath, and consume $W_{\mathrm{in}}>0$. Define its cooling coefficient of performance by $\mathrm{COP}_R=Q_c/W_{\mathrm{in}}$. Then
$
\mathrm{COP}_R\le\frac{T_c}{T_h-T_c}.
$
Equality holds exactly when the total entropy change of the isolated compound is zero. A reversible cycle in the stated boundary model saturates the bound; no converse about reversibility is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A cyclic working system with $0<T_c<T_h$, $Q_c>0$, $Q_h>0$, $W_{\mathrm{in}}>0$, no unlisted transfers, and the full working system, baths, and work store inside the declared isolated compound.

[F1] [[def-td-reservoir-cycle]]: In refrigerator mode $Q[P]=Q_c-Q_h$, $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=W_{\mathrm{in}}$, the cold and hot bath energy changes are $-Q_c$ and $+Q_h$, their endpoint entropy changes are $-Q_c/T_c$ and $+Q_h/T_h$, and the work store has zero entropy change. The full compound has the admitted equilibrium endpoint record and additive entropy split required by the definition.

[F2] [[post-td-first-law-energy]]: For an admitted closed fixed-constitution process with zero endpoint changes in separately tracked center-of-mass kinetic and external-potential energies, $\Delta U=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$.

[F3] [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]: For an admitted isolated compound process with equilibrium endpoints and the declared additive total entropy, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0$; an admitted reversible operation has $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=0$.

## Proof

- If energy exchange is permitted, $T_A=T_B$.
- If volume exchange is permitted, then $p_A/T_A=p_B/T_B$; if energy exchange is also permitted, this gives $p_A=p_B$.
- If species $j$ can be exchanged, then $\mu_{A,j}/T_A=\mu_{B,j}/T_B$; if energy exchange is also permitted, this gives $\mu_{A,j}=\mu_{B,j}$.

The pressure equality concerns the derivative-defined pressures of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. A retained volume or species constraint supplies no corresponding equality.

## Proof

1.1 For energy exchange choose an arbitrary sufficiently small $h$ joules and the feasible curve $x_A(t)=(U_A^*+t h,V_A^*,n_A^*)$, $x_B(t)=(U_B^*-t h,V_B^*,n_B^*)$ for $t$ near $0$. By [A1], $g(t):=S_A(x_A(t))+S_B(x_B(t))$ has a local maximum at $0$; [F1] and [F3] specify that this thermal energy exchange is allowed. For $t>0$, $(g(t)-g(0))/t\le0$; for $t<0$, the same quotient is $\ge0$. Its derivative exists by [F2], so the two one-sided limits force $g'(0)=0$. The chain rule [L1] gives $g'(0)=h(S_{A,U}-S_{B,U})$. Since $h\ne0$, $S_{A,U}=S_{B,U}$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, L1, construct]

2.1 By [F4], $S_{i,U}=1/T_i$ for $i=A,B$. The temperatures are finite and positive, so equality of their reciprocals gives $T_A=T_B$. [given, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If volume exchange is permitted, hold the energy and species partitions fixed and vary $V_A(t)=V_A^*+t k$, $V_B(t)=V_B^*-t k$ for an arbitrary sufficiently small nonzero volume increment $k$. When energy exchange is also permitted, step 2.1 gives $T_A=T_B>0$, hence $p_A=p_B$. By [A2], this is equality of the two derivative pressures with their respective mechanical piston pressures whenever that coupling applies to each subsystem. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, F4, F5, L1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 If species $j$ is permitted to cross the partition, hold other coordinates fixed and vary $n_{A,j}(t)=n_{A,j}^*+t q$, $n_{B,j}(t)=n_{B,j}^*-t q$ for a sufficiently small nonzero mole increment $q$. Both signs are feasible by hypothesis, so the same derivative argument as in step 1.1 gives $S_{A,n_j}=S_{B,n_j}$. By [F4], $-\mu_{A,j}/T_A=-\mu_{B,j}/T_B$; when energy exchange is also permitted, step 2.1 gives equal positive temperatures and hence $\mu_{A,j}=\mu_{B,j}$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, L1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 If a volume or species coordinate is retained by the definition of $\mathcal F$, its corresponding two-sided feasible curve does not exist. The derivative argument above therefore yields no equality for that coordinate. Boundary points are also excluded by the stated local two-sided feasibility hypothesis. [given, F1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Remark

**Scope.**

Use the fields and local-equilibrium regime of [[rem-td-local-equilibrium-branch]]. A Fourier heat-transport model may postulate

$$\mathbf j_Q(\mathbf x,t)=-K(\mathbf x,t)\nabla T(\mathbf x,t),$$

where $\mathbf j_Q:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is a continuous heat-energy flux field in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and $K:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is a declared conductivity tensor with units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. In an isotropic model $K=\kappa I_3$ with $\kappa\ge0$. A diffusion model may separately postulate $\mathbf j_n=-D\nabla n$, where number density $n:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, number flux $\mathbf j_n:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $D$ is a declared scalar or tensor in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

These are constitutive choices for specified material, geometry, regime, field regularity and boundary conditions. A collision invariant in a kinetic model is a quantity preserved by each allowed collision. Near-equilibrium linear response, a dilute-gas Boltzmann model, a relaxation-time approximation, and a quantum transport model have different hypotheses and coefficient definitions. The relaxation-time approximation can fail to preserve collision invariants; a coefficient derived in one approximation is not thereby universal. Onsager reciprocity is a relation among linear-response coefficients under a specified microscopic time-reversal and conjugate-force convention; this remark does not assert it without those hypotheses. Microscopic calculations and measurements may determine or test coefficients for a specified model and material, but neither the equilibrium entropy postulates nor dimensional consistency alone determine them.

Any heat equation or transport conclusion additionally needs the relevant conservation balance, sources or work terms, constitutive relation, initial data and boundary conditions. No such evolution equation, Onsager relation, or transport coefficient is proved or adopted by this remark.

The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable. ## Facts & Assumptions

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation above.

Both the interval integral and the tail integral in $\eta(g)$ tend to zero as $g\to\infty$, so $\eta(g)\to0$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 For $m\geq2$ and $r\in[(m-1)g,mg]$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(mg)$ and $r^{d-1}\geq((m-1)g)^{d-1}$. 1.3 For integer $m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(m-1)$ on $[m-2,m-1]$, so $\int_{m-2}^{m-1}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq(m-2)^{d-1}\psi(m-1)$. Since $m^{d-1}\leq c_d(m-2)^{d-1}$ for these $m$, summing over disjoint unit intervals proves $\sum_{m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil} m^{d-1}\psi(m-1)<\infty$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 For each integer $k\geq1$, let $G_k$ be the least integer greater than $2R_0$ such that $\eta(g)\leq k^{-2d}$ for every $g\geq G_k$; it exists by step 1.1 and the well-ordering of the positive integers. Therefore $$ \left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\leq k(\ell)^d k(\ell)^{-2d}=k(\ell)^{-d}\to0. $$ This gives all three gap limits. [F1, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Fix distinct points $x,y$ in a finite configuration and a period $L>0$. For $|k|_\infty$ larger than $2|x-y|_\infty/L+2R_0/L$, the triangle inequality gives $|x-y+Lk|_\infty\geq L|k|_\infty/2>2R_0$. There are finitely many remaining images; any $+\infty$ term makes the periodic energy $+\infty$ by definition, while otherwise their finite sum is well-defined. ## Statement

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], fix $\beta>0$, and define $Z(L,N;\beta)$ as in that definition. For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define
$$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$. On the interior of $\{\rho:F(\rho)>-\infty\}$, $F$ is finite and continuous. For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Stability with constant $B$, a regular even pair potential, fixed $\beta>0$, and the free-cube canonical convention in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]].

[F1] Stability gives $U_N\geq-BN$ for every finite configuration; regularity gives an integrable decreasing two-sided tail envelope ([[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]).

[F2] For every sufficiently large gap $g$, the lattice-shell interaction tail is bounded by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]], with a diagonal choice $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$ and vanishing cross-energy density.

[F3] The Lebesgue box and product-measure suppliers give volume $L^{dN}$ for the $N$-fold cube and permit factorization over disjoint cores ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F4] The factorial and logarithm suppliers give the integral bounds $\int_1^m\log x\,dx\leq\log(m!)\leq\int_1^{m+1}\log x\,dx$ and $\log(1+u)\leq u$ for $u>-1$ ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).

The vacuum term gives $b(0)=0$: $Z(L,0)=1$ is a lower bound, and the same stability estimate with $N/L^d\to0$ gives a nonpositive upper limit. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 The effective domain of $F$ has nonempty interior. Fix a core cube of side $s>0$ and a gap $g>R_0$; place one particle in each selected core of a lattice of spacing $s+g$ inside a large box. The absolute interaction from any one occupied core to all others is bounded by $C\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2]. Restricting each particle to a subcube of volume $v_0>0$ therefore gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\geq v_0^N e^{-C_0N}$ for every density strictly below $(s+g)^{-d}$, after omitting unused lattice cells. Thus $F$ is finite on a nonempty interval of positive densities; by its definition as a finite-mixture envelope it is concave. [F1, F2, F3, algebra, construct]

2.1 Fix a finite list of core preparations $(s_i,n_i)$ with $0<Z(s_i,n_i;\beta)<\infty$. Exact factorization over disjoint core cubes follows because assigning the labeled coordinates to their cores contributes $N!/\prod_i(n_i!)^{M_i}$, cancelling the global $N!$. [F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For any finite convex combination in the definition of $F(\rho)$, choose core preparations with densities tending to its $\rho_i$ and rates tending to $b(\rho_i)$. If their effective densities do not strictly bracket the target $\rho$, add arbitrarily small weights at one attainable density below and one above $\rho$; such densities exist because $\rho$ is interior. Their mixture coefficients can then be perturbed by quantities tending to zero so the effective mean is exactly $\rho$. Place the fixed core types in finitely many macroscopic slabs with these volume fractions, inserting fixed empty layers wider than $R_0$ between slabs. [F1, F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 First reserve an outer layer of fixed width $W$ and adjust slab fractions in the remaining volume to match the target density; the strict bracketing in step 3.1 absorbs the reserved layer's $O(WL^{d-1})$ volume without assuming its one-particle capacity replaces a bulk density. This establishes finiteness and continuity of $F$ on its effective interior while leaving excluded endpoints undecided. [F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. For free-boundary cubes define $\Xi_L(a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$. Then
$$1\leq\Xi_L(a,\beta)\leq\exp(ae^{\beta B}L^d),\qquad p(a,\beta):=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(a,\beta)$$
exists and is finite. This theorem assumes only stability and the decreasing integrable two-sided tail in regularity; it does not assert canonical fixed-density convergence, periodic-boundary equality, or arbitrary-region limits.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Dimension $d\geq1$, a stable regular pair potential, its stability constant $B$, and fixed numerical length and energy units.

[A1] Stability means $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration, and the grand partition uses the $1/N!$ normalization in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]].

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: for some nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi$ and $R_0<\infty$, $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ for $|x|_\infty\geq R_0$, with finite weighted integral $\int_{R_0}^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}dr$.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]: $\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g)$ and there are gaps $g(\ell)$ with $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$ and $(\ell/g(\ell))^d\eta(g(\ell))\to0$.

[F3] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]: $|[0,L)^d|=L^d$ and finite product Lebesgue measure gives $|([0,L)^d)^N|=L^{dN}$.

[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]], [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], and [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]: the nonnegative exponential series sums to $e^x$, $0!=1$, and nonnegative grand terms may be split into a finite partial sum and its tail.

[F5] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative sums and product integrals factor over finitely many disjoint regions.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Put $q=ae^{\beta B}$. For every $N$-point configuration, $0\leq e^{-\beta H_\phi}\leq e^{\beta BN}$ by [A1]. Applying [F3] to the finite-volume integral gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Summing by [F4] yields $\Xi_L\leq e^{qL^d}$; the empty configuration contributes exactly $1$, so $\Xi_L\geq1$. [A1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Choose $K>eq+1$ and an integer cutoff $n_\ell$ with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$. For $N>n_\ell$, $1\leq e^{N-K\ell^d}$, so $$ \sum_{N>n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)\leq e^{-K\ell^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eq\ell^d)^N}{N!}=e^{(eq-K)\ell^d}\leq e^{-\ell^d}. $$ Because $\Xi_\ell\geq1$, the truncated sum $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)$ satisfies $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix a core side $\ell$ and a gap $g>2R_0$. Place $M=\lfloor L/(\ell+g)\rfloor^d$ disjoint core cubes of side $\ell$ in $[0,L)^d$ on the lattice of spacing $\ell+g$. Restrict every core to at most $n_\ell$ particles. If two core indices differ by maximum norm $m\geq1$, every pair between them has separation at least $mg$ in maximum norm. The number of offsets in shell $m$ is $(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d\leq c_dm^{d-1}$. By [F1], the sum of positive cross-core pair energies is therefore at most $$ D_{L,\ell,g}\leq c_dM n_\ell^2\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Negative cross-core energies only increase the Boltzmann weight. Splitting the grand sum by the particle counts in these disjoint cores, Tonelli [F5] and the multinomial coefficient show that the global $N!$ cancels the assignments of labeled coordinates to cores. Thus $$ \Xi_L\geq e^{-\beta D_{L,\ell,g}}(\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut})^M. $$ [F1, F3, F5, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Divide the last inequality by $L^d$ and let $L\to\infty$ with $\ell,g$ fixed. Since $M/L^d\to(\ell+g)^{-d}$, [F2] gives $$ \liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L\geq\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g}\right)^d\left[\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-C_dK_1^2\left(\frac{\ell}{g}\right)^d\eta(g)\right], $$ where $K_1=K+1$ bounds $n_\ell/\ell^d$ for $\ell\geq1$ and $C_d$ absorbs the fixed shell-count constant and $\beta$. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The numbers $p_\ell=\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell$ lie in $[0,q]$ by step 1.1, so choose $\ell_j\to\infty$ with $p_{\ell_j}\to\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. Set $g=g(\ell_j)$ from [F2]. Then $g/\ell_j\to0$, the volume fraction tends to $1$, the cutoff logarithm divided by $\ell_j^d$ tends to zero, and the cross-core error tends to zero. Step 4.1 therefore yields $\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\geq\limsup_{L\to\infty}p_L$. The reverse inequality is automatic for every real sequence, so the limit exists; step 1.1 makes it finite. [F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Extend it by $F_\beta(0)=0$, by its interior upper-semicontinuous limit at any finite upper endpoint of its effective domain, and by $-\infty$ outside the closed effective domain; retain the value $-\infty$ if the endpoint limit is $-\infty$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$. These are thermodynamic limits of positional partition functions. They do not assert local-observable equivalence, a finite-volume endpoint realization, or a thin energy-shell limit.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A stable regular pair potential, $\beta>0$, its free-cube canonical partition functions, and the exact entropy/rate conventions above.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]: for each interior attainable $\rho>0$ and every sequence $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, $L^{-d}\log Z(L,N_L;\beta)\to F_\beta(\rho)$; the proof supplies the slab-packing inequality and sparse low-density lower bound.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]: stability bounds the grand tail exponentially and the free-cube grand-pressure limit exists for every positive activity.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-finite-dimensional-biconjugation]]: a proper closed convex function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space equals its biconjugate under the stated extended-real conventions.

[A1] Stability supplies a finite $B\geq0$ with $U_N\geq-BN$ ([[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Fix an interior attainable density $\rho>0$ and a sequence $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. The grand sum contains the nonnegative term $e^{\alpha N_L}Z(L,N_L;\beta)$, so $\liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta)\geq F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho$ by [F1]. Taking the supremum over interior densities gives the lower bound. The vacuum term $Z(L,0)=1$ gives the value $0$ at density zero. Endpoint values are limits from the interior by their definition, so they do not enlarge the supremum. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Put $q=e^{\alpha+\beta B}$. For each $N\geq0$, stability and the box-volume formula give $e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Choose $K>eq+1$. For $N>KL^d$, $1\leq e^{N-KL^d}$, so the factorial bound gives $\sum_{N>KL^d}e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta) \leq e^{-KL^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eqL^d)^N}{N!} \leq e^{-L^d}.$ The remaining at most $KL^d+2$ terms are bounded by their maximum times this number; its logarithm divided by $L^d$ tends to zero. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Choose maximizing retained particle numbers and a subsequence with $N_L/L^d\to\rho\in[0,K]$; nested-interval bisection on the compact interval $[0,K]$ supplies the subsequence. The canonical upper rate is at most $b(\rho)\leq F_\beta(\rho)$, since the one-term mixture in the definition of $F_\beta$ includes $b(\rho)$. At $\rho=0$, stability gives upper rate at most $0=F_\beta(0)$. If $u$ is a finite upper endpoint and $b(u)>-\infty$, mix a preparation approaching $b(u)$ with an interior preparation of density $r<u$, in slab fractions $1-\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$. The exact packing inequality in [F1] gives $F_\beta((1-\epsilon)u+\epsilon r)\geq(1-\epsilon)b(u)+\epsilon b(r).$ As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, the left side tends to the assigned interior endpoint limit; hence $b(u)\leq F_\beta(u)$. If $b(u)=-\infty$ this bound is automatic. Outside the closed effective domain, $b(\rho)=-\infty$, again because a finite $b(\rho)$ would make $F_\beta(\rho)\geq b(\rho)$. Thus the maximum retained term has limiting rate at most $\sup_{\rho\geq0}(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho)$. The tail estimate in step 1.2 and the lower bound in step 1.1 prove the first equality. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The extension $F_\beta$ is proper, upper-semicontinuous and concave. It is finite and concave on its open effective interior by [F1], hence continuous there. At zero, stability and the concavity of $g(\rho)=\rho(1+\beta B-\log\rho)$ give $F_\beta(\rho)\leq g(\rho)\to0$. The sparse separated-cell lower bound in [F1] gives $F_\beta(\rho)\geq c\rho$ for a fixed finite $c$, so $F_\beta(\rho)\to0=F_\beta(0)$. At any finite upper endpoint use the assigned interior upper-semicontinuous limit; outside the closed effective domain set $F_\beta=-\infty$. Hence $G=-F_\beta$, with $G=+\infty$ on negative densities, is a proper closed convex extended-real function on $\mathbb R$. Its conjugate is $G^*(\alpha)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\{\alpha\rho+F_\beta(\rho)\}=P(\alpha,\beta)$ by steps 1.1–2.2. Applying [F3] gives $G(\rho)=\sup_\alpha\{\alpha\rho-P(\alpha,\beta)\}$, which is the second equality. The endpoint convention is needed for closedness; it asserts no finite-volume endpoint realization. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$ be superstable in the splitting convention of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The potential and splitting above.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: superstability supplies a stable part and a nonnegative repulsive part bounded below by $\delta$ on a fixed neighborhood of the origin.

## Proof

**Given:** The assumptions and the half-open unit-cell partition.

## Example

In one dimension, let the pair potential be infinite when the separation is less than $a>0$, and zero otherwise. For $N\geq1$ labeled rods in $[0,L]$, with canonical positional normalization $1/N!$, write $S=L-(N-1)a$. If $S>0$, translating the ordered coordinates by $y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$ gives
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac{S^N}{N!}=\frac{(L-(N-1)a)^N}{N!},\qquad \beta>0.$$
If $S=0$, the allowed configuration set has zero Lebesgue measure and $Z(L,N;\beta)=0$. Along $N\to\infty$ with $L=(N-1)a$, the density $N/L\to1/a$ while every finite-volume partition is zero. Thus the thermodynamic close-packing endpoint is approached by a sequence of zero-weight finite systems; it is not realized by a positive canonical partition. The interior canonical limit theorem makes no assertion at that endpoint.
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Hard-core distance $a>0$ and inverse temperature $\beta>0$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: the canonical positional partition integrates over labeled coordinates and divides by $N!$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]: its canonical limit assertion is restricted to interior attainable densities.

[F3] [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: product Lebesgue measure assigns volume $S^N$ to the cube $[0,S]^N$ and permits iterated integration.

[F4] [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]: the coordinate-order partition has $N!$ permutation chambers and the canonical normalization divides by $N!$.

[F5] [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]: translating a Lebesgue-measurable set preserves its Lebesgue measure.


## Proof

**Given:** $N\geq1$ and $L\geq(N-1)a$.

1.1 Order the coordinates $0\leq x_1<\cdots<x_N\leq L$. The exclusion constraints are $x_{i+1}-x_i\geq a$. Apply the coordinatewise translation $x_i\mapsto y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$; each one-coordinate translation preserves Lebesgue measure [F5], so product measure is preserved. The ordered region becomes $0\leq y_1\leq\cdots\leq y_N\leq S$, where $S=L-(N-1)a$. The cube $[0,S]^N$ splits, up to equality sets of zero product measure, into $N!$ coordinate-order regions. Product-measure uniqueness makes these permutation chambers equal in measure, so the ordered region has volume $S^N/N!$. The full labeled allowed volume is $N!$ times this, and canonical division by $N!$ gives $Z(L,N;\beta)=S^N/N!$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 If $L=(N-1)a$, then $S=0$ and the transformed region is a null set; its integral is zero. If $L>(N-1)a$, then $S>0$ and the ordered region has positive product volume. Thus the maximal-density endpoint does not carry a positive canonical partition at exact close packing; the interior-only theorem [F2] makes no contrary assertion. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty set of system types, $X_i$ a nonempty state set with chosen reference $r_i\in X_i$ for each $i\in I$, and $M$ a common meter state set with $z_0,z_1\in M$. Assume for every $i$ that the product state set $X_i\times M$ satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]], with strict reference pair $(r_i,z_0)\prec\prec(r_i,z_1)$. Let $S_i$ be its normalized representation and put $\sigma_i(x):=S_i(x,z_0)$. In that product comparison, the unit product-state point mass satisfies $e_{(x,z_0)}\sim_s(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{(r_i,z_0)}+\sigma_i(x)e_{(r_i,z_1)}$, by [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. These product-state point masses are distinct from the shared state-and-meter compounds defined next.

Assume in addition a **common-meter compatibility interface**. Let $\mathcal Y$ contain disjoint families of raw state tags $a_{i,x}$, raw type-reference tags $\rho_i$, and two distinct raw meter tags $\zeta_0,\zeta_1$. Using the unit point masses on these tags, write $e_{r_i}:=e_{\rho_i}$ and $e_{z_j}:=e_{\zeta_j}$, and define $u_{i,x}:=e_{a_{i,x}}+e_{z_0}$. Thus $u_{i,x}$ is an explicit mass-two state-and-fixed-meter compound; it is not a unit tag. Compounds over $\mathcal Y$ use the finite-support convention of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]], and their signed comparison is the one in [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]. Require the exact substitution

$$u_{i,x}\sim_s e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x)e_{z_1}\qquad(i\in I,\ x\in X_i),$$

finite substitutions to compose, and the fixed reference sum $\sum_iT_ie_{r_i}$ to cancel when type totals agree. Both sides of this signed substitution have total coefficient two, even when $\sigma_i(x)$ lies outside $[0,1]$. Require the common meter point masses to satisfy $e_{z_0}\preceq e_{z_1}$ and not $e_{z_1}\preceq e_{z_0}$. These are hypotheses on the comparison algebra, not consequences of separate numerical meter readings.

For positive coefficients $t_{ik}$ on a finite collection of type-$i$ states $x_{ik}$, define $T_i:=\sum_k t_{ik}$ and $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Put $C_0:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}e_{a_{i,x_{ik}}}$ and $C:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}u_{i,x_{ik}}=C_0+T e_{z_0}$. Thus $C_0$ is the state compound of mass $T$ and $C$ is its fixed-meter encoding of mass $2T$. Empty collections give $T=0$ and $C_0=C=0$. Define

$$\Sigma(C):=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_k t_{ik}\sigma_i(x_{ik}).$$

For two such compounds $C,D$ with the same type-total vector $(T_i)_{i\in I}$, the common comparison satisfies $C\preceq D$ exactly when $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Equivalently, the same order criterion holds for the state compounds $C_0,D_0$ after canceling their common $T e_{z_0}$. The index family is finite; no arbitrary-index choice or infinite decomposition is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The common-meter compatibility interface in the Statement: the exact signed substitution for every $u_{i,x}$ holds, finite substitutions compose, equal type totals give the same cancellable reference sum, and the common meter pair is strict.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] supplies the real normalized product representation, and [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]] supplies $e_{(x,z_0)}\sim_s(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{(r_i,z_0)}+\sigma_i(x)e_{(r_i,z_1)}$ in its unit product-state comparison. The separate mass-two shared substitution is exactly [A1], not an identification of different product and shared tags.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]: finite signed substitutions are additive and common terms can be canceled. [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] and [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] also preserve signed comparison under positive scaling: multiplying the difference by a positive scalar multiplies both its positive and negative parts by that scalar, so the compound scaling axiom applies.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-reference-order]]: for the common strict meter pair, comparison of equal-mass reference expressions is exactly comparison of their $z_1$ coefficients.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F3].

1.1 For each constituent $(i,x_{ik},z_0)$ of $C$, its mass-two shared compound $u_{i,x_{ik}}$ is equivalent by the exact substitution in [A1] to $e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x_{ik}))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x_{ik})e_{z_1}$. Each side has total coefficient two, so this signed substitution is defined. Scale by $t_{ik}>0$ and combine the finitely many comparisons using [A1] and [F2]. The resulting reference-system part is $\sum_iT_i e_{r_i}$, independent of the chosen states. The meter part has coefficients $T-\Sigma(C)$ on $e_{z_0}$ and $\Sigma(C)$ on $e_{z_1}$, where $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Hence $C$ is equivalent to that fixed reference-system compound plus $(T-\Sigma(C))e_{z_0}+\Sigma(C)e_{z_1}$, whose total coefficient is $T+T=2T$. If the collection is empty, both expressions are zero and the equivalence is reflexivity, requiring no order scaling at zero. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The same substitution for $D$ gives the same reference-system compound because its type totals are the same, and the same total meter mass $T$. Cancel the common reference-system terms by [A1] and [F2]. If $T>0$, the remaining meter expressions have total coefficient $T$; positive scaling by $1/T$ turns them into the unit reference maps $R_{\Sigma(C)/T}$ and $R_{\Sigma(D)/T}$. By [F3] these compare exactly when $\Sigma(C)/T\le\Sigma(D)/T$, which is equivalent to $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Scaling back by $T>0$ proves the reverse comparison equivalence, so no unit-mass reference theorem is applied directly at mass $T$. Reversing the same equivalences proves the converse implication as well. Since $C=C_0+T e_{z_0}$ and $D=D_0+T e_{z_0}$, [F2] also gives $C\preceq D$ exactly when $C_0\preceq D_0$; for $T=0$ all these compounds are empty and the criterion is $0\le0$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Remarks

The compatibility interface records the compositional assumption needed to move from separate product systems to one shared meter scale. Without it, independent representations need not share a multiplicative calibration. This theorem makes no statement for infinitely many types.

## Example

Take two types with fixed totals $T_1=T_2=1$ and a common meter satisfying the compatibility hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-common-meter-calibration]]. Let type-1 states $a_0,a_1$ have normalized values $0,1$, and type-2 states $b_0,b_1$ have normalized values $1/3,3$. Using the shared raw state tags of that theorem, let $C_0=e_{a_{1,a_1}}+e_{a_{2,b_0}}$ and $D_0=e_{a_{1,a_0}}+e_{a_{2,b_1}}$. Their fixed-meter encodings are $C=C_0+2e_{z_0}$ and $D=D_0+2e_{z_0}$, each of mass four. The calibrated values are $4/3$ for $C$ and $3$ for $D$; the common-meter comparison orders $C\preceq D$ and, after common-meter cancellation, $C_0\preceq D_0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The fixed type totals and values in the Example: one unit of each type, with $\sigma_1(a_1)=1$, $\sigma_1(a_0)=0$, $\sigma_2(b_0)=1/3$, and $\sigma_2(b_1)=3$.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-common-meter-calibration]]: under its finite common-meter compatibility assumptions, a compound comparison is equivalent to comparing the sum of its typewise calibrated values.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]: normalized values are real and may lie outside $[0,1]$ for states other than the two references.

## Verification

**Given:** [A1], [F1], and [F2].

1.1 Both compounds have type-total vector $(1,1)$, so [F1] applies. Their calibrated values are $\Sigma(C)=1+1/3=4/3$ and $\Sigma(D)=0+3=3$. Since $4/3\le3$, [F1] gives $C\preceq D$. The theorem also cancels their common $2e_{z_0}$, giving $C_0\preceq D_0$. The value $3$ is permitted by [F2]; the representation theorem imposes no unit-interval bound on arbitrary states. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Reversing the comparison would require $3\le4/3$, which is false; hence this particular comparison is strict. No separate per-type numerical reading is treated as a proof of common-meter compatibility; that remains the stated hypothesis. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For finite random variables $M,R$ with joint law $p(m,r)$ and marginals $p_M,p_R$, use the entropy definition $H(Y)$ of [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]] for $Y=M,R,(M,R)$. Define $I(M;R):=\sum_{p(m,r)>0}p(m,r)\log\frac{p(m,r)}{p_M(m)p_R(r)}$. Then $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)=H(M)-H(M|R)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $p(m,r)=p_M(m)p_R(r)$ for every pair.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $p(m,r)$ is a joint probability law on finite sets and $p_M,p_R$ are its marginal laws.

[F1] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-finite-sum]]: the joint and marginal probabilities are finite normalized sums, and if $p(m,r)>0$ then both marginals are positive.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]]: finite Shannon entropies are defined there and satisfy $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log t$ is differentiable for $t>0$ with derivative $1/t$.

[F4] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: derivative signs determine monotonicity on an interval.

## Proof

**Given:** A finite joint law $p(m,r)$ and its two marginals.

1.1 Define $\phi(t):=t-1-\log t$ for $t>0$. Its derivative is $1-1/t$, nonpositive on $(0,1]$ and nonnegative on $[1,\infty)$; the mean-value theorem [F4] gives $\phi(t)\ge\phi(1)=0$, with equality only at $t=1$. Thus $-\log t\ge1-t$, strictly unless $t=1$. [F3, F4]

1.2 Expanding the finite logarithmic sum gives $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)$; applying [F2] rewrites it as $H(M)-H(M|R)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Put $q(m,r):=p_M(m)p_R(r)$. For $p(m,r)>0$, $q(m,r)>0$ by [F1], and step 1.1 with $t=q/p$ gives $p\log(p/q)\ge p-q$. Summing over the support of $p$ yields $I(M;R)\ge1-\sum_{p>0}q\ge0$. Equality forces $q=p$ on the support and no $q$-mass outside it, hence equality at every pair; conversely independence makes each positive logarithm zero. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-mutual-information]]: $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)=H(M)-H(M|R)$.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]]: conditional entropy is computed from the conditional laws on positive-probability register values.

[A1] The pair law assigns probability $1/2$ to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and zero to the other two pairs.

## Example

Let $M,R\in\{0,1\}$ have joint probabilities $p(0,0)=p(1,1)=1/2$ and $p(0,1)=p(1,0)=0$. Then $H(M)=H(R)=\log2$, $H(M,R)=\log2$, $H(M|R)=0$, and $I(M;R)=\log2$.

## Verification

**Given:** The finite joint probability law in [A1].

1.1 Both marginals are uniform, so their entropies are $-2(1/2)\log(1/2)=\log2$. The joint law has two positive entries of size $1/2$, so $H(M,R)=\log2$. [A1, algebra]

1.2 Conditional on either value of $R$, $M$ is determined, so its conditional law has one probability $1$ and one $0$; therefore $H(M|R)=0$. Substituting these values into [F1] gives $I(M;R)=\log2$. [F1, F2, A1, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Then $Z$ is positive, finite, and $C^2$ on $J$, with $Z'(\beta)=-\sum_i g_iE_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ and $Z''(\beta)=\sum_i g_iE_i^2\exp(-\beta E_i)$. The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized; their mean $\bar E$ and variance are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]: $Z$, $p_i$, expectation, variance and $H_g$ have the definitions and domains stated there.

[F2] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $\exp$ is positive and differentiable with $\exp'=\exp$.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log$ is defined on positive reals and $(\log u)'=u'/u$ for differentiable $u>0$.

[F4] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior has a point where its secant slope equals its derivative.

[A1] For every compact $K\subset J$ there is a nonnegative summable sequence $(a_i)$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)e^{-\beta E_i}\le a_i$ for all $i$ and $\beta\in K$; the tail $\sum_{i>N}a_i$ tends to zero.

[F5] [[thm-chain-rule]]: differentiating $e^{-\beta E_i}$ with respect to $\beta$ uses the one-variable chain rule.

## Proof

**Given:** The countable canonical model and the local summable envelope in the statement.

1.1 On a compact interval $K\subset J$, let $Z_N$, $D_N$, and $Q_N$ be the first $N$ partial sums of $\sum_i g_i e^{-\beta E_i}$, $-\sum_i g_iE_ie^{-\beta E_i}$, and $\sum_i g_iE_i^2e^{-\beta E_i}$. 1.2 For an interior $\beta$ and sufficiently small $h\ne0$, apply [F4] to $Z_N$ on the interval with endpoints $\beta$ and $\beta+h$: its difference quotient is $D_N(\xi_{N,h})$ for some intermediate $\xi_{N,h}$. Applying the same argument to $D_N$ and $Q_N$ proves $D'=Q$, so the displayed derivatives hold. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

2.1 The summands of $Z$ are positive and at least one is present, hence $0<Z<\infty$ on $K$; summing the definition of $p_i$ gives $\sum_i p_i=1$. 3.1 Since $p_i/g_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$, its logarithm is $-\beta E_i-\log Z$. The finite first moment makes $\sum_i p_i|\log(p_i/g_i)|\le |\beta|\sum_i p_i|E_i|+|\log Z|\sum_i p_i<\infty$; summing the identity gives $H_g=\beta\bar E+\log Z$. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]: finite canonical probabilities are normalized exponential weights.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]: the finite canonical partition sum and its normalized law are valid whenever $Z$ is positive and finite.
